question: France has accumulated an additional EUR 900 billion of debt since 2017, its government deficit reached at least 4.9 % of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2023 and the country’s debt burden will rise to EUR 57 billion in 2024.

If Moody’s and Fitch, or Standard & Poor’s lower France’s rating on 26 April or 31 May respectively, this would further undermine the credibility of Emmanuel Macron and his government, as well as their ability to govern France. In light of this, the Finance Committee of the French Senate conducted a review of the Ministry of Economy and criticised the French government for ‘withholding information’.

They noted that if the deficit continues to slip away from the government’s control, in 2024 and 2025, it is predicted to reach 5.7 % and 5.9 % of GDP respectively. The official statistics passed on to the Commission however, were 4.4 % and 3.7 %.

In view of this catastrophic budgetary management by the government – which is proving incapable of adhering to the fiscal path it ensured was adopted by invoking Article 49.3 of the Constitution – and given the disconnect between the deficits that have been announced and those that are now envisaged: 1.
Does the Commission think that the French government may have been negligent or insincere when it drew up its last budget?
Does it plan on launching an infringement procedure against France for excessive deficit in the near future?
answer: The Commission’s Spring 2024 Economic Forecast (1) projects that France’s economy will grow by 0.7% in 2024 and 1.3% in 2025; public deficit will be 5.3% in 2024 before decreasing to 5.0% in 2025; public debt will stand at 112.4% in 2024 before growing to 113.8% in 2025.

As part of the Spring package, the Commission has adopted a report (2) under Article 126(3) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, examining the reasons for the excess over the 3% of gross domestic product deficit threshold in several Member States, including France. Subsequently, on 8 July 2024 the Commission adopted proposals to the Council under Article 126(6) on the existence of an excessive deficit (3).
Now the procedure will continue, culminating with the Council taking a decision.
